newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Hill-Govt rides blows on Maori TV.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Hill-Govt rides blows on Maori TV.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Feb 19 - It was the political eqivalent of Muhammad Ali's "rope a dope'.

Faced with unfinished probes by Commerce officials and the Serious Fraud Office into Aotearoa Television and the possibility the opposition has more muck to rake, the New Zealand coalition government has opted to ride the blows, taunting its critics to land a knockout punch in the hope there is not a haymaker around the corner.
Parliament's first sitting day of 1997 on Tuesday saw more of the same.

First the government asked for a snap debate in an attempt to take the initiative. That failed because Alliance leader Jim Anderton refused leave -- he wanted to debate patient safety at Christchurch hospital.

When Labour got the nod from the speaker for its written request for a debate on Aotearoa, the government put up Commmunications Minister Maurice Williamson and then gave Labour, Act and the Alliance a free hand until Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters took the final call -- predictably to claim no serious blows had been landed.

His only tactical error was to refuse Labour's Trevor Mallard leave to table a document showing shareholding changes in the Aotearoa group involving trust companies. Mallard said these changes coincided with embattled New Zealand First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan's exit from the company. The documents are public and Mallard was raising questions about their import rather than presenting "proof" as such. By refusing leave, Peters weakened his argument that the opposition had not presented a scrap of evidence. It is something he plans to rectify today by allowing the documents to be tabled.

The debate itself saw little new evidence, but put into the public arena rumours that have been circulating in parliament for weeks. While Labour's Helen Clark raised some questions about directors' spending to add to the now legendary $89 underpants bought by Morgan, she tried to refocus the debate on ministerial responsibility and the cabinet decision to first fund Aotearoa TV and then reverse that decision two weeks later. It is an area ripe for mining, given the shifting defences the government has used.

Why, for instance, did Williamson and Prime Minister Jim Bolger make much play of the Treaty of Waitangi obligation, crystallised by the courts, to fund Maori television if the decision was so easily reversed?

If all was well at Aotearoa, why was "greater discipline" required of Aotearoa after October 31 "than it has shown to this point" as the Commerce Ministry noted in its briefing to Williamson on August 19? If, as Williamson said, they were just teething troubles, what are the specifics?

Again, if the taxpayer got what was contracted for -- and more -- from the station, what did the Commerce Ministry mean in the same document when it said Maori funding agency Te Mangai Paho had acknowledged "there had been difficulties of several kinds both with Aotearoa Television Network as a provider and with the nature of the programming which it has provided"?

Moreover, the government will find it hard to convince the public it should have reversed a decision to fund the station if, as it also claims, everything was going well; especially when its advice was to ensure improvements in financial management at the station before granting future funding -- some
way short of pulling the plug altogether.

The current parliamentary fracas aside, it is an issue that will not go away. Mallard has said it could take a year for all the facts to come out and Peters has begun the groundwork for an exit should the heat get too intense.
Talking to journalists before parliament resumed, he was careful to qualify his stance.

He said the New Zealand First caucus had heard an explanation from Morgan and was satisfied with it. "He gave a very full explanation in which he regreted any embarrassment there may have been ... to the Maori people and to the party and
thanked the party profusely for standing behind him in a series of allegations all of which to this point in time seem to be baseless ... and I emphasise this point in time."
As Peters has said in recent months, circumstances change.
